column1: Adult patient with abdominal pain W9F4N2K7C6RM
column3:
Axial arterial-phase T1 C+ MR in a hypercoagulable patient shows multiple hypervascular foci . Some of the lesions seem to have a hypointense rim, while others have a hypointense central scar .
Axial T1 C+ MR in a hypercoagulable patient 2 hours after IV administration of gadobenate dimeglumine shows persistent uptake and retention of the agent within the nodules , indicating functional hepatocytes and deficient biliary ducts within the lesions.
Axial T1 C+ MR in a patient with Budd-Chiari syndrome shows multiple hypervascular nodules , some of which have a central scar . These multiple large, regenerative nodules (nodular regenerative hyperplasia) confirmed transplantation.
Axial CECT in a patient with Budd-Chiari syndrome and nodular regenerative hyperplasia shows a central scar and doughnut-like enhancement. Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) is also seen .
In this patient with Budd-Chiari syndrome and multiple hypervascular nodules, trichrome stain shows green staining of the central scar and the capsule of the nodule, typical features of the macroscopic form of nodular regenerative hyperplasia or large regenerative nodules.

column11: Why does FNH retain hepatobiliary contrast while its central scar does not?
column12: The source states that FNH can retain hepatobiliary contrast more than liver, while the central scar does not take up or retain gadoxetate. Outside clarification: this contrast behavior reflects functioning hepatocytes in FNH and a central scar/septal component that does not function like the surrounding hepatocellular tissue. Imaging pivot: lesion-level hepatobiliary retention with scar nonretention supports FNH over adenoma.

column11: Why does a cavernous hemangioma show peripheral nodular enhancement with progressive fill-in?
column12: The source describes nonscarred hemangioma tissue as showing peripheral nodular enhancement with progressive fill-in and very high T2 signal. Outside clarification: cavernous hemangioma is made of blood-filled vascular spaces, so contrast first opacifies peripheral vascular lakes and then progressively fills central spaces. Imaging pivot: blood-pool-like peripheral nodular enhancement separates hemangioma from most solid tumors.

column11: Why is portal-vein tumor invasion such a strong clue for conventional HCC in this pattern?
column12: The source states that large conventional HCC may be heterogeneous and hypervascular with washout, central necrosis or scar, and common vascular invasion/metastases. Portal-vein tumor invasion converts a scar-mimicking hypervascular mass from a broad differential into a strongly HCC-favored pattern. Imaging pivot: tumor-in-vein is more specific than the central scar-like region itself.
